'''Network Data Envelopment Analysis''' (Network DEA) is an advancement of the traditional [[Data envelopment analysis|Data Envelopment Analysis]] (DEA) methodology,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Charnes |first1=A. |last2=Cooper |first2=W. W. |last3=Rhodes |first3=E. |date=1978 |title=Measuring the efficiency of decision making units |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |volume=2 |issue=6 |pages=429–444 |doi=10.1016/0377-2217(78)90138-8 |doi-access=free }}</ref> designed to evaluate the efficiency of [[Data envelopment analysis|Decision-Making Units]] (DMUs) by accounting for their internal structures. Unlike classical DEA, which treats DMUs as "[[Black box|black boxes]]," Network DEA decomposes them into interconnected subsystems or stages, providing a more detailed and accurate assessment of their operations.

== Background ==
The conventional DEA models assume that DMUs operate as single-stage processes, ignoring the internal structures. These limitations gave rise to Network DEA, that extends traditional DEA by considering a DMUs as a system with sub-processes, i.e.,the DMUs are modeled as networks of interconnected stages, each with its own inputs, outputs, and intermediate products. An indicative example of such a DMU is a [[supply chain]], which has a [[Network theory|network structure]] and is composed of several members whose performances affect the overall performance of the supply chain.

Intermediate products are internal measures that simultaneously act as outputs of some stages and inputs of some others. Their treatment differentiates network DEA models from conventional DEA formulations.

In addition, the efficiency is assessed at both the system (overall DMU) and stage levels. The earliest network DEA formulations appeared in studies of multi-stage production systems. Initial models focused primarily on two-stage structures, while later works generalized to series, parallel, and dynamic network configurations.

Reviews and classifications of network DEA methods can be found in the literature.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last1=Castelli |first1=L. |last2=Pesenti |first2=R. |last3=Ukovich |first3=W. |date=2010 |title=A classification of DEA models when the internal structure of the decision making units is considered |journal=Annals of Operations Research |volume=173 |issue=1 |pages=207–235 |doi=10.1007/s10479-008-0414-2 |hdl=10278/24242 |hdl-access=free }}
</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last1=Cook |first1=W. D. |last2=Liang |first2=L. |last3=Zhu |first3=J. |date=2010 |title=Performance of two-stage network structures by DEA: A review and future perspective |journal=Omega |volume=38 |issue=6 |pages=423–430 |doi=10.1016/j.omega.2009.12.001 }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Agrell |first1=P. J. |last2=Hatami-Marbini |first2=A. |date=2013 |title=Frontier-based performance analysis models for supply chain management: State of the art and research directions |journal=Computers & Industrial Engineering |volume=66 |issue=3 |pages=567–583 |doi=10.1016/j.cie.2013.02.014 }}</ref><ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last1=Halkos |first1=G. E. |last2=Tzeremes |first2=N. G. |last3=Kourtzidis |first3=S. A. |date=2014 |title=A unified classification of two-stage DEA models |journal=Surveys in Operations Research and Management Science |volume=19 |issue=1 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.1016/j.sorms.2013.10.001 }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Kao |first=C. |date=2014 |title=Network Data Envelopment Analysis: A Review |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |volume=239 |issue=1 |pages=1–16 |doi=10.1016/j.ejor.2014.02.039 }}</ref><ref name="Koronakos2019" />

== Overview ==
Network DEA extends traditional DEA by considering a DMUs as a system with [[Subprocess|sub-processes]], i.e.,the DMUs are modeled as networks of interconnected stages, each with its own inputs, outputs, and intermediate products. Intermediate products are internal measures that simultaneously act as outputs of some stages and inputs of some others. Their treatment differentiates network DEA models from conventional DEA formulations. In addition, the efficiency is assessed at both the system (overall DMU) and stage levels.

The earliest network DEA formulations appeared in studies of multi-stage production systems. Initial models focused primarily on two-stage structures, while later works generalized to series, parallel, and dynamic network configurations.

Several reviews and classifications of network DEA methods have been published.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref name=":4" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name="Koronakos2019">{{cite book
 |last=Koronakos
 |first=G.
 |chapter=A taxonomy and review of the network data envelopment analysis literature
 |title=Machine Learning Paradigms: Applications of Learning and Analytics in Intelligent Systems
 |year=2019
 |pages=255–311
}}</ref>

== Major Network DEA assessment paradigms ==
The following categorization of Network DEA assessment paradigms is made in:<ref name="Koronakos2019"/>

* Efficiency Decomposition:<ref>Kao, C., & Hwang, S. N. (2008). Efficiency decomposition in two-stage data envelopment analysis: An application to non-life insurance companies in Taiwan. European journal of operational research, 185(1), 418-429.</ref><ref>Chen, Y., Cook, W. D., Li, N., & Zhu, J. (2009). Additive efficiency decomposition in two-stage DEA. European journal of operational research, 196(3), 1170-1176.</ref><ref>Liang, L., Wu, J., Cook, W. D., & Zhu, J. (2008). The DEA game cross-efficiency model and its Nash equilibrium. Operations research, 56(5), 1278-1288. </ref><ref>Chen, Y., Du, J., Sherman, H. D., & Zhu, J. (2010). DEA model with shared resources and efficiency decomposition. European journal of operational research, 207(1), 339-349.</ref> The efficiency decomposition approach first evaluates the overall efficiency of the DMU and subsequently derives the efficiencies of the individual stages through a decomposition mechanism.

* Efficiency Composition:<ref>Despotis, D. K., Koronakos, G., & Sotiros, D. (2016). Composition versus decomposition in two-stage network DEA: a reverse approach. Journal of productivity Analysis, 45(1), 71-87.</ref><ref>Despotis, D. K., Sotiros, D., & Koronakos, G. (2016). A network DEA approach for series multi-stage processes. Omega, 61, 35-48.</ref><ref>Despotis, D. K., Koronakos, G., & Sotiros, D. (2016). The “weak-link” approach to network DEA for two-stage processes. European Journal of Operational Research, 254(2), 481-492.</ref> The composition approach evaluates the efficiencies of the individual stages first and then aggregates them to determine the overall system efficiency.

* Slack-Based Measures (SBM):<ref>Tone, K., & Tsutsui, M. (2009). Network DEA: A slacks-based measure approach. European journal of operational research, 197(1), 243-252.</ref><ref>Tone, K., & Tsutsui, M. (2010). Dynamic DEA: A slacks-based measure approach. Omega, 38(3-4), 145-156.</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fukuyama |first1=H. |last2=Weber |first2=W. L. |date=2010 |title=A slacks-based inefficiency measure for a two-stage system with bad outputs |journal=Omega |volume=38 |issue=5 |pages=398–409 |doi=10.1016/j.omega.2009.10.006 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Fukuyama |first1=H. |last2=Mirdehghan |first2=S. M. |date=2012 |title=Identifying the efficiency status in network DEA |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |volume=220 |issue=1 |pages=85–92 |doi=10.1016/j.ejor.2012.01.024 }}</ref> The SBM approach simultaneously determines both stage and overall efficiencies by directly incorporating input and output slacks into the assessment mode.

* System-centric:<ref>Färe, R., & Whittaker, G. (1995). An intermediate input model of dairy production using complex survey data. Journal of Agricultural Economics, 46(2), 201-213.</ref><ref>Löthgren, M., & Tambour, M. (1999). Productivity and customer satisfaction in Swedish pharmacies: A DEA network model. European Journal of Operational Research, 115(3), 449-458.</ref><ref>Färe, R., & Grosskopf, S. (2000). Network dea. Socio-economic planning sciences, 34(1), 35-49.</ref> The system-centric approach considers the internal structure and interdependencies of the subprocesses while providing only a single overall efficiency measure without explicitly estimating stage efficiencies.

== Applications ==
Network DEA has broad applicability in sectors where internal processes significantly impact performance, including:

*Supply Chains: Evaluating efficiency across multiple stages of production and distribution.<ref name=":1" />
*Healthcare Systems: Analyzing hospitals or departments with interdependent operations<ref>Chilingerian, J. A., & Sherman, H. D. (1990). Managing physician efficiency and effectiveness in providing hospital services. Health Services Management Research, 3(1), 3-15.</ref>
*Education: Assessing universities by decomposing activities such as teaching and research<ref>Avkiran, N. K. (2009). Opening the black box of efficiency analysis: an illustration with UAE banks. Omega, 37(4), 930-941.</ref>
*Energy Systems: Studying multi-stage energy production and distribution processes<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cong |first1=D. |last2=Liang |first2=L. |last3=Han |first3=Y. |last4=Han |first4=Y. |last5=Geng |first5=Z. |last6=Chu |first6=C. |date=2021 |title=Energy supply efficiency evaluation of integrated energy systems using novel SBM-DEA integrating Monte Carlo |journal=Energy |volume=231 |article-number=120834 |doi=10.1016/j.energy.2021.120834 |bibcode=2021Ene...23120834C }}</ref>

== Limitations ==
Despite its advantages, Network DEA (NDEA) presents several limitations. The incorporation of internal structures substantially increases model complexity and computational burden, especially in generalized multi-stage or network configurations. In addition, several studies<ref name=":1" /> have noted that standard DEA projection mechanisms are not always directly applicable in two-stage or network settings because efficient frontier determination and projection consistency become more difficult when intermediate measures connect stages. Another important limitation concerns the treatment of returns to scale.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Banker |first1=R. D. |last2=Thrall |first2=R. M. |date=1992 |title=Estimation of returns to scale using data envelopment analysis |journal=European Journal of Operational Research |volume=62 |issue=1 |pages=74–84 |doi=10.1016/0377-2217(92)90178-C }}</ref> In some NDEA formulations, the implementation of VRS is problematic.<ref name=":1" /><ref name="Despotis2025">{{cite journal
 |last1=Despotis
 |first1=D. K.
 |last2=Sotiros
 |first2=D.
 |last3=Koronakos
 |first3=G.
 |title=Data Envelopment Analysis of two-stage processes: An alternative (non-conventional) approach
 |journal=International Transactions in Operational Research
 |year=2025
 |volume=32
 |issue=1
 |pages=384–405
|doi=10.1111/itor.13320
 |doi-access=free
 }}</ref> Finally, decomposition of overall efficiency into stage efficiencies may not always be unique, leading to ambiguity in the interpretation of divisional performance scores.<ref name="Despotis2025"/>
